top_stories.title: Binance $6.3-6.4 Billion Hack: Attack Chain, Attribution, and Recovery
points: Attack began with a fake job interview/recruiter targeting a Binance developer with a trojan-laced coding assignment, tied to North Korea's TraderTraitor hacking group.

Attackers distributed a poisoned developer tool (compromised software appearing legitimate but containing malicious code) to deepen access, then used an internal AI tool to compromise two more engineers and steal wallet signing credentials.
The campaign spanned five months before escalating into the theft.
Attackers exploited Ethereum's EIP-7702 (an upgrade letting ordinary wallets run smart contract code) to gain partial control of a hot wallet holding billions.
Total theft reached $6.34-6.4 billion, among the largest crypto hacks on record.
Binance has recovered or frozen approximately $2.85 billion and replenished 98% of stolen assets with help from law enforcement and blockchain analytics firms.
North Korea denies involvement; Kim Yo Jong called the FBI's attribution a 'grave political provocation' and suggested the U.S. could be responsible.

unique_angles.point: Blockchain forensics firms TRM and Chainalysis tied the hack specifically to North Korea's TraderTraitor group based on patterns from previous crypto thefts.
Fake recruiter campaigns and malware-laden developer tools are an established North Korean tactic, though the scale of this hack is unprecedented.

items.title: Tether's Bitcoin Holdings Reach ~150,000 BTC
points: Tether, issuer of the USDT stablecoin (a digital currency designed to maintain a fixed value, typically pegged to the U.S. dollar), now holds approximately 150,000 bitcoin, a notable concentration for a stablecoin issuer.

items.title: Liquid Network Fully Restores Bitcoin Backing
points: Blockstream's Bitcoin sidechain Liquid Network restored full backing two months after a $320 million exploit.
CEO Adam Back cautioned developers against blindly trusting AI-generated security fixes.

AI is expected to expose long-tolerated security flaws in infrastructure systems.

issues.subject: 👀 Binance's $6.34B Hack Began With a Fake Job Interview

headlines: Binance's $6.34 billion hack stemmed from a five-month social engineering campaign that began with a fake job interview and a poisoned developer tool, according to the exchange's incident report.

Tether now holds approximately 150,000 bitcoin, representing a significant concentration of the cryptocurrency by a stablecoin issuer (a digital currency designed to maintain a fixed value, typically pegged to the U.S. dollar).

sections.title: Binance Hack: Five-Month Social Engineering Campaign
points: 1. Attack started with a fake job interview used to target a Binance developer, establishing initial access to the organization.
2. Hackers distributed a poisoned developer tool (compromised software that appeared legitimate but contained malicious code) that gave them deeper system access over five months.
3. The total theft reached $6.34 billion before Binance detected and contained the breach.

headlines: Binance's $6.4 billion hack traced to fake job interview where North Korean attackers targeted engineers with malware-laced coding assignments, then escalated to steal wallet credentials via internal AI tools.

sections.title: How Binance Was Hacked: The Full Attack Chain
points: 1. Initial compromise: fake recruiter convinced a Binance engineer to download a trojan-laced coding "assignment" in September using tactics linked to North Korea's TraderTraitor group.
2. Lateral movement: attackers leveraged the internal AI tool to compromise two additional engineers' computers and steal credentials to Binance's wallet signing service.
3. Exploitation: attackers used Ethereum's EIP-7702 (an upgrade allowing ordinary wallets to run smart contract code) to gain partial control of a hot wallet holding billions.
4. Recovery: Binance has already restored 98% of assets; law enforcement and blockchain analytics firms helped freeze or intercept approximately $2.85 billion of the stolen funds.

sections.title: North Korea's Response and Attribution
points: 1. Pyongyang's denial: Kim Yo Jong called the FBI's attribution a "grave political provocation" and suggested the U.S. could be behind the theft to deflect blame.
2. Analyst consensus: blockchain forensics firms TRM and Chainalysis have tied the hack to North Korea's TraderTraitor group, linking it to patterns of previous cryptocurrency thefts.
3. Tactics signature: fake recruiter campaigns and malware-laden developer tools are established North Korean methods, though the $6.3-6.4 billion scale is unprecedented.
